Figure 19. State-level D3 metrics of the single-family detached for load shifting, 1 hour, 2°F offset 4.6 Limitations and Concerns In this measure, demand response is dispatched every day. This is done to evaluate and estimate the potential impact of demand response over a wide range of day types and weather conditions. For this reason, although the individual day-level results for this measure are realistic, the annual energy consumption savings are not consistent with the current dispatch practices, and they should not be used directly. Instead, users interested in estimating annual energy impacts should splice daily time-series results from the baseline model (without demand response) and the time-series results from the upgraded model (with demand response) in the target proportion. This measure is applied to all dwelling units with electric heating or cooling to investigate load flexibility potential; however, only a subset of these units is ideally suited for this measure. Units already equipped with smart thermostats have a lower barrier to entry into a demand response program. This measure assumes that units without a smart thermostat would be equipped with one as part of the installation process. Alternately, utilities could ask customers to manually adjust thermostats for a small number of events per year, but the participation of such a program would be important to establish. If one wishes to study the impact of the partial penetration of smart thermostats or less than 100% participation in the demand response program, they should take a subset of buildings from the upgrade and take the rest from the baseline. In previous calibration efforts, the building energy models used in ResStock have shown a temperature decay that is faster than empirical data. To better match the empirical data, ResStock uses an increased thermal capacitance multiplier for the air inside the dwelling units.
